recipes.name: Lạng Sơn Egg Rice Rolls
recipes.description: A Lạng Sơn specialty of thin rice sheets wrapped around a softly cooked egg, served with hot pork-bone broth, minced pork and fried shallots. Bếp Việt adapts the steaming method to a lidded nonstick pan for home cooks.
recipes.serving_basis: 4 servings, each with hot egg rice rolls and a bowl of pork-bone broth.
recipes.finished_dish: Soft, thin rice wrappers enclose a tender egg and are served with clear, aromatic broth, fried shallots and tangy pickled bamboo shoots.
recipes.serving: Arrange the rolls on small plates and serve the hot broth alongside or spooned over to taste. Eat while the egg is still soft with pickled bamboo shoots and cilantro.
tips: Keep the batter thin enough to spread; stir before each roll because rice flour settles.
Cover briefly so the white sets while the yolk stays soft; cook longer if you prefer a firm yolk.
Prepare and keep the broth hot, then cook the rolls just before serving so they do not dry out.
recipes.image_alt: Lạng Sơn egg rice rolls with thin rice wrappers, soft yolks, pork-bone broth and pickled bamboo shoots.
recipes.time_note: Bếp Việt adapts the traditional cloth steamer to a lidded nonstick pan; adjust steaming time for wrapper thickness and preferred egg doneness.
search_terms: rice rolls with hot bone broth
ingredients: Adds a tender, slightly chewy texture.
Use fresh eggs, one per roll.
Some for the broth and some for frying.
Serve on the side to taste.
preparation_steps: Whisk the rice flour, tapioca starch, water and 3 g salt until smooth. Rest for 20 minutes, then stir again. Blanch the bones and rinse away the foam.
Chop the shallots. Prepare the eggs, fried shallots, cilantro and pickled bamboo shoots; set out a steamer or lidded nonstick pan.
cooking_steps: Simmer the bones in about 1.5 litres of water over low heat for 35–40 minutes, skimming as needed. Fry some shallot, add the ground pork and cook until loose, then add it to the broth. Season with fish sauce, salt and pepper.
Heat a nonstick pan and brush it lightly with oil. Add a ladle of batter and swirl into a thin layer. Crack an egg into the centre, cover and steam for 45–75 seconds until the white sets.
Fold the wrapper around the egg and transfer carefully to a plate. Repeat for each serving. Pour over hot broth, top with fried shallots and cilantro, and serve with pickled bamboo shoots.

recipes.name: Thanh Hóa Bitter Leaf Soup
recipes.description: A soup associated with Mường communities in the Thanh Hóa highlands, known for a gentle bitterness followed by a clean sweetness. Bếp Việt’s home version uses thoroughly cleaned chicken offal, chicken and a little fermented rice, with an option to reduce the leaves for first-time tasters.
recipes.serving_basis: 4 bowls, served hot as part of a family meal.
recipes.finished_dish: A dark-green soup fragrant with lemongrass, tender chicken and offal, and a clear bitter-leaf finish softened by a little fermented-rice tang.
recipes.serving: Ladle into bowls while hot, dividing the meat and broth evenly. Serve as a soup with rice; offer extra chili or fermented rice on the side for a stronger flavour.
tips: Buy edible bitter leaves from a trusted source; do not forage wild leaves unless you can identify them with certainty.
Clean the chicken offal thoroughly and cook it completely; use chicken meat alone for a milder soup.
Start with fewer leaves, taste and add more gradually; overcooking can make the leaves mushy and the bitterness harsh.
recipes.image_alt: A bowl of Thanh Hóa bitter leaf soup with chicken offal and meat, dark green leaves and a little red chili.
recipes.time_note: Preparation time depends on cleaning the chicken offal. Substitute chicken meat alone for a quicker, milder version.
search_terms: bitter leaf soup with chicken offal
ingredients: Wash several times and slice; reduce to 60 g for a milder taste.
Clean thoroughly and cut into bite-size pieces.
Strain and add gradually for gentle tang.
preparation_steps: Rinse the chicken offal thoroughly, remove any residue, rub lightly with salt, rinse and cut into small pieces. Rinse and dice the chicken.
Remove tough stems from the bitter leaves, wash them well and slice. Bruise the lemongrass, chop the shallot and strain the fermented rice with a little water.
cooking_steps: Sauté the shallot and lemongrass in a little oil until fragrant. Add the chicken offal and chicken; stir-fry until the surface turns opaque. Season lightly with salt and pepper.
Add 900 ml water, bring to a boil, then lower the heat. Simmer until the chicken and offal are fully cooked, about 10–12 minutes, skimming if needed.

Stir in the strained fermented rice a little at a time and taste for gentle acidity. Add the bitter leaves and simmer for 3–5 minutes until just tender. Season with fish sauce, add optional chili and serve hot.

recipes.name: Hải Dương Field Perch Noodle Soup
recipes.description: A bowl from the former Hải Dương region pairs boiled and deboned field perch, lightly fried until golden, with fish-bone broth and greens such as water celery or mustard greens. Bếp Việt uses cleaned perch, carefully checks for bones and keeps the broth delicately seasoned.
recipes.serving_basis: 4 hot bowls, each with field perch, greens and broth.
recipes.finished_dish: White rice vermicelli in a light golden fish broth topped with golden perch, tomato, green water celery and fragrant herbs.
recipes.serving: Blanch the vermicelli and divide among bowls with quickly blanched water celery or greens. Add the fried fish, pour over hot broth and finish with scallions and dill. Serve promptly to keep the fish crisp.
tips: Buy properly cleaned perch from a trusted fishmonger and check carefully for bones; simmer the head and bones in a filter bag for the broth.
Fry the fish in a properly heated pan and turn gently so the pieces stay intact.
Do not overcook the greens; blanching separately keeps their colour bright and the broth clear.
recipes.image_alt: A bowl of Hải Dương field perch noodle soup with golden fried perch, green water celery, tomato and clear broth.
recipes.time_note: Prep time assumes the fish has been cleaned by the fishmonger. Allow extra time to clean it yourself and remove bones carefully.
ingredients: Ask the fishmonger to clean it; keep head and bones for stock.
Wash and cut into short lengths.
preparation_steps: Rinse the cleaned fish in lightly salted water and rinse again. Cut the water celery, tomatoes, scallions, dill and ginger; separate the flesh from the head and bones.
Season the fish flesh with half the shallots, a little salt, pepper and turmeric for 10 minutes. Rinse the vermicelli if needed and drain.
cooking_steps: Poach the fish in 1.8 litres water with ginger until just cooked. Remove and cool, pick the meat and check it carefully for bones. Put the head and bones in a filter bag and simmer for 15 more minutes, then discard the bag.
Sauté the remaining shallots, add the tomatoes and cook until softened. Stir them into the fish stock. Season with fish sauce, salt and pepper, then keep at a gentle simmer.
Toss the fish lightly with a little oil and pan-fry until golden on both sides. Quickly blanch the water celery in the broth; blanch the vermicelli separately and divide into bowls.
Top the vermicelli with fish, pour over the broth and tomatoes, add the greens and finish with scallions and dill. Serve hot.

recipes.name: Lạng Sơn Mugwort Rice Cakes
recipes.description: A Tày specialty from Lạng Sơn: chewy green glutinous-rice cakes coloured and scented with mugwort leaves, often filled with sugar, sesame and peanuts. Bếp Việt uses vegetable oil instead of animal fat, making this home version suitable for a vegetarian meal; the cakes are best eaten the day they are made.
recipes.serving_basis: 12 small mugwort cakes with sesame-peanut filling, best eaten the same day.
recipes.finished_dish: Deep-green, flattened glutinous-rice cakes with a soft, chewy wrapper and a fragrant brown-sugar, sesame and peanut filling.
recipes.serving: Lightly brush the cakes with oil, arrange on clean banana leaves and serve while soft. They pair well with hot tea and need no dipping sauce.
tips: Choose tender mugwort leaves, wash well and cook until very soft before pounding or blending; do not use concentrated limewater.
Knead while the leaves are still warm, adding hot water a little at a time until the dough is pliable but not sticky.
Fresh cakes are best the same day. Wrap leftovers airtight, refrigerate and steam again before serving.
recipes.image_alt: Deep-green Lạng Sơn mugwort cakes made with glutinous rice; one is cut open to show brown-sugar, sesame and peanut filling on banana leaf.
recipes.time_note: This home adaptation uses thoroughly cooked mugwort and vegetable oil. Glutinous rice flour absorbs water differently, so add hot water gradually.
ingredients: Pick young leaves and remove tough stems.
Reserve a little to adjust the dough.
Add gradually; you may not need all of it.
For hands and cakes; keeps the recipe vegan.
preparation_steps: Wash the mugwort leaves several times and boil for 20–25 minutes until tender. Rinse, squeeze dry and pound or blend with a little hot water.
Toast the sesame and crush the peanuts. Melt the brown sugar with 1–2 tablespoons water, stir in the sesame, peanuts and dried coconut, then cool and divide into 12 filling balls.
cooking_steps: Combine the blended mugwort with the glutinous rice flour and salt. Add hot water gradually and knead to a smooth, pliable dough that does not stick to your hands. Cover and rest for 10 minutes.
Divide into 12 portions and roll into balls. Flatten each, enclose one filling ball, seal the edges and pat into a round about 1 cm thick.
Arrange on lightly oiled banana leaves and steam for 10–12 minutes until glossy and cooked through. Brush lightly with oil and serve warm.

recipes.name: Sa Đéc Hu Tieu Noodle Soup
recipes.description: Sa Đéc hu tieu is known for smooth white rice noodles that stay tender without turning mushy, served in a light pork-bone broth. Bếp Việt’s home version uses dried shrimp for depth and tops the bowl with pork and fresh shrimp; traditional broth may be simmered longer.
recipes.serving_basis: 4 bowls of rice-noodle soup with pork, shrimp and a light broth.
recipes.finished_dish: A bowl of tender white rice noodles in a clear, gently sweet broth, topped with sliced pork, shrimp, bean sprouts and fresh garlic chives.
recipes.serving: Briefly blanch the hu tieu noodles and divide among bowls. Arrange the pork, shrimp, bean sprouts and chives on top, then ladle over piping-hot broth. Serve lime, chili and soy sauce on the side.
tips: Use Sa Đéc rice noodles if available; follow the package directions and do not soak too long or they may turn mushy.
Simmer the bones gently and skim regularly for a clear, delicate broth.
Offer greens, lime, chili and soy sauce at the table; keep the broth light rather than overly sweet.
recipes.image_alt: A bowl of Sa Đéc hu tieu rice noodles with sliced pork, shrimp, bean sprouts, garlic chives and clear broth.
recipes.time_note: This home version simmers the bones for about an hour to save time. Traditional stock may be cooked longer; adjust blanching to the noodles you use.
ingredients: Use Sa Đéc noodles if available; soak or blanch as directed.
Peel and devein; keep shells for the stock if desired.
preparation_steps: Blanch the pork bones for 3 minutes, discard the water and rinse. Rinse and soak the dried shrimp; peel the daikon and char the onion lightly.
Thinly slice the pork. Peel and devein the shrimp; wash and drain the bean sprouts, chives, scallions, lime and chili. Prepare the noodles according to the package directions.
cooking_steps: Put the bones, dried shrimp, daikon, onion and 2.2 litres water in a pot. Bring to a boil, skim, then simmer gently for about 60 minutes. Strain and season with salt, fish sauce, rock sugar and pepper, keeping the broth delicate.
Add the pork to the gently simmering broth and cook just through; remove and slice if needed. Cook the shrimp in the broth for 2–3 minutes until pink, without overcooking.

Briefly blanch the hu tieu noodles in boiling water according to the package directions and drain. Divide them among bowls with bean sprouts, chives, pork and shrimp; ladle over hot broth and top with scallions.
Serve immediately with lime, chili and soy sauce for each diner to season at the table.
